newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Japan finalises laws aimed at MOF's power.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Japan finalises laws aimed at MOF's power.

text.p: Japan on Monday finalised bills aimed at trimming the mighty Finance Ministry's power by boosting the central bank's independence and creating a new financial supervision agency, government officials said.

Analysts, however, expressed some doubt as to whether the elite MOF, whose image has been dented by allegations of policy missteps, would be much chastened or lose much real influence as a result of the changes.
Japan's cabinet on Tuesday is expected to approve reforms to a law governing the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) independence, the first such change in almost five decades.

The cabinet will also approve bills to deprive the Finance Ministry of its authority to inspect and supervise financial firms and bestow that role on a new Financial Supervision Agency to be set up between April 1, 1998 and July 1, 1998
Parliament is expected to pass both laws this session.
Politicians, ostensibly keen to pry power out of the hands of bureaucrats, have grappled with both issues since 1995.

That was when public outrage erupted over the ministry's handling of a string of banking failures, the Daiwa Bank bond loss debacle and a plan to use tax money to help wind up mortgage firms which collapsed under heaps of bad loans left when Japan's late 1980s asset price "bubble" burst.

The public ire, fueled by scandals involving senior Finance Ministry bureaucrats, renewed debate over the merits of breaking up the ministry, which not only oversees financial institutions but also controls budget formation and taxation.

Proponents of changes to the decades-old BOJ legal framework, which critics say at times left the bank prey to pressure from politicians and finance bureaucrats to keep credit loose, also seized on the public anger as providing a chance to boost central bank independence.

Under Finance Ministry reform bills, an independent agency will be set up under the Prime Minister's Office to oversee financial institutions, although the trade, labour and agriculture ministries will share supervision of some firms.

The new agency would be responsible for handling financial failures, but would consult with the finance minister in cases where an order to halt business or a revocation of a licence would have a serious impact on the financial system as a whole.

Under BOJ law revisions, the government will no longer be able to order the central bank to postpone decisions on monetary policy. The government will still be able to intervene in monetary policy decisions by asking the BOJ policy-making board to delay them, but the board will have the ultimate say.

The reforms also obligate the BOJ to testify on its monetary policies at parliament whenever required and to submit to parliament a report on its decisions on monetary policy approximately every six months.

Some economists lauded both the BOJ law reform and the creation of the new financial supervision agency as steps toward a more independent central bank and a potentially more efficient system for financial institution oversight.

"The question is whether the institutional separation of functions (between the new supervisory agency and MOF) will result in a more effective bureaucratic structure. I think to a certain extent the answer is 'yes,'" said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

Referring to the BOJ law reforms, Feldman said, "I think it's a step in the right direction but we have to see how it operates in practice and how independent the new board will be, and we won't know until some conflict comes up."
Others expressed greater doubt that the Finance Ministry would lose much as a result of either reform.

"Whether or not the LDP (ruling Liberal Democratic Party) wanted to strip MOF of influence is still a question, given that they keep appointing ministry bureaucrats to key areas of reform deliberations," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan. "But whether they wanted to or not, they are totally incapable of doing so."
